meta.title: Where Does Rain Come From?
meta.textType: functional: a school science text with headings and a diagram, for the class blog

paragraphs: Posted by Lily. On Wednesday, February third, our class studied rain in the science lesson. Teacher Kim drew a diagram on the whiteboard. It had four labels: "SUN," "SEA," "CLOUD," and "RAIN." Curved arrows went from one label to the next. Mia, Leo, May, and I sat at our desks with our notebooks. "Today we study physics," said Teacher Kim. "Physics is the science of heat and movement." "Where does rain come from?"

Next, Teacher Kim did a short experiment. She put a small pot of hot water on the table. "The water is nearly one hundred degrees," she said, so we stood a step back. Then she held a cold metal plate above the pot. Soon small drops of water hung under the plate. "When the warm air is cooled, drops are made," said Teacher Kim. "The reason is simple: cold air holds less water." "Clouds are made in the same way, but high in the sky."

This is my science page for the blog. Its title is "Our Science Page," and it has three headings. The first heading is "The sun heats the sea." First, the water of the ocean and the sea is warmed, and it goes up into the air. Heating changes the water, so we cannot see it in the air. The second heading is "Clouds are made." Next, the warm air is cooled high in the sky, and small drops are made. Many, many small drops make a cloud. The third heading is "Rain falls." Finally, the drops become heavy, and rain falls. A very big cloud can bring a storm.

"Where does the water go after the rain?" asked Mia. "Back to the sea, along the rivers," said Leo. "Yes," said Teacher Kim. "The same water goes around again and again," she said. "It is a circle in nature," she added. "The sun, the air, and the sea work together."

February is in the dry season. Still, Teacher Kim looked out of the window. "It may rain tomorrow," she said. "Is that a fact or a guess?" asked Leo. "It is a guess," said Teacher Kim, "because the clouds are gray." I wrote everything in my notebook, because my memory is not perfect. "Maybe the water in my bottle was in the ocean once," said Mia. Teacher Kim smiled. "It may be true," she said.

sentences.text: Posted by Lily.
On Wednesday, February third, our class studied rain in the science lesson.
Teacher Kim drew a diagram on the whiteboard.
It had four labels: "SUN," "SEA," "CLOUD," and "RAIN."
Curved arrows went from one label to the next.
Mia, Leo, May, and I sat at our desks with our notebooks.
"Today we study physics," said Teacher Kim.
"Physics is the science of heat and movement."
"Where does rain come from?"
Next, Teacher Kim did a short experiment.
She put a small pot of hot water on the table.
"The water is nearly one hundred degrees," she said, so we stood a step back.
Then she held a cold metal plate above the pot.
Soon small drops of water hung under the plate.
"When the warm air is cooled, drops are made," said Teacher Kim.
"The reason is simple: cold air holds less water."
"Clouds are made in the same way, but high in the sky."
This is my science page for the blog.
Its title is "Our Science Page," and it has three headings.
The first heading is "The sun heats the sea."
First, the water of the ocean and the sea is warmed, and it goes up into the air.
Heating changes the water, so we cannot see it in the air.
The second heading is "Clouds are made."
Next, the warm air is cooled high in the sky, and small drops are made.
Many, many small drops make a cloud.
The third heading is "Rain falls."
Finally, the drops become heavy, and rain falls.
A very big cloud can bring a storm.
"Where does the water go after the rain?" asked Mia.
"Back to the sea, along the rivers," said Leo.
"Yes," said Teacher Kim.
"The same water goes around again and again," she said.
"It is a circle in nature," she added.
"The sun, the air, and the sea work together."
February is in the dry season.
Still, Teacher Kim looked out of the window.
"It may rain tomorrow," she said.
"Is that a fact or a guess?" asked Leo.
"It is a guess," said Teacher Kim, "because the clouds are gray."
I wrote everything in my notebook, because my memory is not perfect.
"Maybe the water in my bottle was in the ocean once," said Mia.
Teacher Kim smiled. "It may be true," she said.
